6 Discussion

This research suggests that integrating VF into residential buildings in hot-arid regions may help reintroduce outdoor living spaces, privacy gradients, and semi-private family areas into vertical housing environments. In the Emirati housing context, the traditional courtyard historically served as a climatic moderator, social space, and private outdoor area. Vertical farming terraces, rooftop gardens, and shared farming floors can therefore be interpreted as a vertical reinterpretation of selected courtyard functions, allowing vertical housing developments to translate some spatial and social characteristics of traditional Emirati housing while responding to land scarcity and urban densification. The use of immersive VR also represents a methodological contribution. In contexts where future housing typologies do not yet exist as built references, as is the case with vertical farming integration in Emirati housing, VR-based participatory evaluation can elicit informed user feedback that conventional drawings, photographs, or physical models may not provide. Participants reported that VR helped them assess spatial proportions, privacy conditions, and outdoor usability more clearly than images alone. This aligns with emerging literature on VR as a participatory design instrument (Shareef and Galal Ahmed, 2024) and suggests that immersive evaluation methods can support pre-design community consultation in the UAE and similar Gulf contexts.

The literature review demonstrated that global vertical farming integration projects such as Bosco Verticale, Tao Zhu Yin Yuan, and Agro-Housing are often discussed in relation to food production, environmental performance, thermal comfort, biodiversity, and social interaction within buildings. Previous studies suggest that integrating vegetation into buildings may improve thermal insulation, reduce cooling loads, enhance air quality, and contribute to urban biodiversity and environmental sustainability (Zhang et al., 2024; Blom et al., 2023; Al-Kodmany, 2018). However, the present study did not directly measure these environmental effects through simulation, monitoring, or performance assessment. Instead, it extends the literature by showing that, in a socio-culturally specific context such as Emirati housing, the perceived value of vertical farming integration is evaluated primarily through social and spatial functions rather than agricultural productivity or measured environmental performance. Participants assessed the proposed scenarios as outdoor living environments, reinforcing the argument that residential vertical farming should first be designed as a socio-spatial strategy, while environmental performance should be validated through future technical studies.

The preference distribution clarifies how participants evaluated the three design strategies. Scenario 3 was selected by 21 out of 30 participants, showing a clear majority preference for the mixed approach, while Scenarios 1 and 2 received lower and relatively similar levels of support. This pattern suggests that neither privacy alone nor hosh-like spatial generosity alone was sufficient. Scenario 1 offered stronger privacy through planted room coverage but was limited by its narrow linear form, while Scenario 2 offered a larger hosh-like terrace but required additional privacy treatment. Scenario 3 was preferred because it combined both qualities within one spatial strategy. The case study analysis of Dibba Al Hosn revealed that one of the major challenges of vertical housing in the UAE is the loss of traditional outdoor spaces such as courtyards, which historically supported family gatherings, planting, and daily activities. Previous research on Emirati public housing has shown that social sustainability is strongly linked to privacy, family interaction, and outdoor space availability (Shareef and Galal Ahmed, 2024). The e-participation findings strongly support and deepen this conclusion. Privacy emerged as the single most influential factor shaping scenario acceptance across both male and female participants, with vegetation alone considered insufficient, particularly at night, and architectural screening elements such as operable mashrabiya-style screens consistently recommended as necessary complements to planting.

The gendered patterns of preference identified in this study carry direct implications for the spatial programming of vertical farming terraces in Emirati housing. Female participants consistently prioritized the cultural legibility of outdoor space as a hosh analogue and its capacity to support family gathering, while male participants foregrounded spatial efficiency, climate-specific usability, and the technical adequacy of privacy screening beyond vegetation alone. These differences suggest that a single undifferentiated terrace typology is unlikely to satisfy both groups simultaneously, and that future design frameworks for Emirati vertical housing should consider gender-responsive spatial differentiation, including the option of gender-segregated gathering zones within shared spaces, as an important design parameter rather than a secondary consideration. This finding extends existing literature on gender and space in Gulf housing contexts by showing that gendered spatial preferences remain important when traditional housing expectations are translated into vertical environments.

The technical framework identifies hydroponic systems supported by drip irrigation or closed-loop fertigation as the most adaptable option for residential integration, while greywater recycling and air-conditioning condensate recovery emerge as more relevant water-reuse strategies than rainwater harvesting in the UAE because rainfall is limited and seasonal. The selected case-study model proposes air-conditioning condensate recovery as a supplementary irrigation source, while treated greywater remains a possible supplementary option subject to treatment and regulatory approval. The Mixed Vertical Farming scenario, which received the strongest overall support, also presents the most complex irrigation demand because it combines private terrace planting, shared intermediate farming floors, and rooftop growing areas. This suggests that automated drip irrigation, centralized water conditioning, and clear maintenance access are important for supporting the social acceptance of the preferred scenario, particularly by reducing the maintenance burden on residents. Without reliable, low-maintenance irrigation infrastructure, the maintenance concerns identified by participants could undermine the long-term viability of the most socially preferred design. This finding reinforces the importance of integrating technical and socio-spatial design considerations from the earliest stages of vertical housing development rather than treating water management as a secondary engineering concern (Matarneh et al., 2024; Al Khoury et al., 2023).

The research also identified practical implementation challenges related to capital cost, irrigation maintenance, nutrient management, water treatment, building infrastructure integration, and long-term management responsibility. Participants expressed concerns regarding maintenance responsibility, insects, cost, and shared-space management, indicating that vertical farming integration should be supported by clear maintenance strategies and dedicated operational frameworks rather than relying on residents alone. The preference expressed by multiple participants for a building-level specialist to oversee shared farming areas reflects a broader pattern in community-based urban agriculture, where collective maintenance is more sustainable when supported by institutional structures rather than voluntary resident participation (Martin et al., 2016). These findings should be interpreted in relation to the methodological, technical, and environmental-performance limitations of the study.

The findings also have policy and spatial-equity implications for UAE affordable/public housing. The proposed VF extensions should be understood as government-supported design alternatives for public housing, not as retrofits that individual residents are expected to fund. Since these projects involve structural additions, rooftop and intermediate-floor farming spaces, waterproofing, safety systems, condensate recovery, filtration, pumps, irrigation networks, and long-term maintenance, the main infrastructure should be planned and supported by housing authorities. The three proposed scenarios can help government decision-makers understand which spatial configurations future users may prefer before implementation. Residents would mainly use and cultivate the private and shared farming spaces provided, while government agencies, municipalities, NGOs, or community organizations could support participation through incentives, starter kits, seedlings, training, farming guidance, and maintenance support. This is important to prevent retrofit and maintenance costs from being transferred unfairly to residents, especially limited-income beneficiaries. Planning guidelines should also define privacy screens, shaded terraces, safe rooftop and intermediate-floor farming areas, drainage, waterproofing, non-potable irrigation systems, maintenance access, and management responsibilities. Shared farming spaces should have clear usage rules to ensure fair access for women, men, children, elderly residents, and different household types. These rules should clarify access schedules, booking systems, gender-sensitive use, children’s safety, crop ownership, and maintenance responsibility. In addition to improving greenery and outdoor use, VF may also support small-scale food production through herbs and vegetables, but actual crop yield, household savings, and food-security benefits should be tested through future pilot projects.

The findings of this study may be analytically transferable to other GCC and hot-arid contexts where vertical housing, land scarcity, high cooling demand, limited outdoor space, and culturally specific privacy expectations shape residential design. However, transferability should not be understood as direct generalization. The Emirati hosh has specific cultural meanings related to family life, privacy, gendered use, hospitality, and outdoor domestic activities, and comparable courtyard or outdoor-space traditions may differ across the Gulf region. Therefore, applying the proposed vertical farming scenarios in other GCC or hot-arid contexts would require adaptation to local family structures, privacy norms, housing policies, building regulations, water-reuse standards, maintenance systems, and climatic conditions. The study’s contribution is therefore most relevant as a transferable design approach: using building-integrated vertical farming to reinterpret culturally valued outdoor living spaces in vertical housing, while adjusting spatial, technical, and regulatory details to each local context.

This study has three main limitations. First, the research was based on a single case study, the Dibba Al Hosn vertical public housing project in Sharjah, and on an intentionally controlled participant sample of Emirati participants aged 20–23. Although this sample was appropriate for exploring the perceptions of a young generation likely to encounter future public housing options during household formation, it does not represent all Emirati age groups, household types, marital statuses, or socio-economic profiles. Future research should therefore examine additional housing typologies, emirates, age groups, and family structures to further validate the proposed vertical farming integration strategies. Second, the user evaluation was conducted through immersive VR-based scenarios rather than through built or occupied vertical farming environments. Although VR enabled participants to compare spatial proportions, privacy relationships, terrace size, greenery, and outdoor-space usability before implementation, it could not reproduce the full sensory and operational conditions of everyday residential use. In particular, the VR evaluation could not simulate thermal comfort under hot-arid outdoor conditions, wind movement, humidity, solar glare, acoustic conditions, smells from planting or irrigation systems, insects, dust, irrigation noise, or the day-to-day effort required to maintain plants, pumps, filters, nutrients, and shared farming areas. It also could not represent temporal changes such as night-time privacy, seasonal heat variation, plant growth, plant decay, or long-term shared-space management. Therefore, the VR findings should be interpreted as perception-based evidence of spatial acceptance rather than proof of long-term residential performance. Future studies should combine VR evaluation with pilot installations, living-lab experiments, environmental monitoring, and post-occupancy assessment. Third, the technical framework requires future validation. The study identifies water-reuse options, irrigation concepts, plant-selection considerations, conceptual sizing, cost implications, and practical implementation constraints, but it does not provide full engineering validation. Detailed structural load calculations, system sizing, crop-yield estimation, energy analysis, code-compliance review, water-quality testing, cost–benefit analysis, operational maintenance planning, and long-term environmental performance simulation remain necessary before implementation. Future research should therefore integrate structural analysis, building-services design, local regulatory review, lifecycle assessment, economic evaluation, environmental simulation, pilot testing, and post-occupancy assessment to evaluate the technical and financial viability of vertical farming systems in hot-arid residential buildings.

From a design perspective, the findings of this research suggest that vertical housing developments in the UAE should incorporate multi-level outdoor spaces rather than relying solely on internal corridors and enclosed apartments. Vertical farming terraces, rooftop gardens, and shared sky courts may function as spatial and environmental buffers, social spaces, and semi-private outdoor areas that support perceived residential quality. The results also indicate that privacy should remain a primary design consideration, and vertical farming elements should be combined with shading devices, screens, and planting buffers to maintain visual privacy. Furthermore, integrating vertical farming systems with building water-reuse systems, particularly greywater reuse and air-conditioning condensate recovery, may support water efficiency in hot-arid climates, although detailed water-balance, environmental-performance, and cost assessments remain necessary before implementation.

7 Conclusion

This study investigated the potential integration of vertical farming systems into vertical residential buildings in hot-arid regions, with a particular focus on the UAE context. The research aimed to develop alternative vertical farming design scenarios suitable for Emirati vertical housing and to evaluate their architectural, socio-spatial, and technical water-reuse implications through literature-informed technical review and e-participation using immersive virtual reality environments. To achieve this aim, the research first reviewed global vertical farming projects and technologies to identify suitable systems for hot-arid climates. Based on this and the technical framework, three alternative scenarios were developed for the Dibba Al Hosn case study: Integrated External, Attached, and Mixed Vertical Farming. These scenarios were modeled using BIM and visualized through Enscape 360° and VR simulations, allowing participants to experience the spaces at a human scale. The results from the e-participation sessions indicated that vertical farming integration is socially acceptable when it supports outdoor living, privacy, greenery, and cultural housing patterns. Privacy, outdoor-space usability, family gathering, and similarity to the traditional hosh were the most important factors influencing participant preferences. Scenario 1, the Integrated External Vertical Farming scenario, was valued for privacy because its long terrace covered the main rooms and created a protective planted edge, but it was considered narrow for family gatherings. Scenario 2, the Attached Vertical Farming scenario, was appreciated for its resemblance to the traditional Emirati hosh because it provided one larger attached outdoor area for seating, planting, and family use, although participants felt that additional privacy treatment would be required. Scenario 3, the Mixed Vertical Farming scenario, received the strongest overall support because it combined the privacy benefits of the integrated terrace with the hosh-like qualities of the attached terrace.

From a technical perspective, the study provides a literature-informed and case-specific assessment of water-reuse and irrigation requirements for the proposed VF scenarios. The analysis suggests that air-conditioning condensate recovery, supported by filtration, storage, nutrient conditioning, and drip/fertigation systems, could help support pilot-scale VF irrigation in hot-arid housing. Rainwater harvesting and greywater recycling remain relevant comparative or supplementary options, but their use depends on rainfall availability, treatment requirements, water quality, regulatory approval, and long-term maintenance. Therefore, the technical findings should be understood as a conceptual integration assessment rather than full engineering validation. Future technical work should test detailed system sizing, structural loading, waterproofing, drainage, MEP coordination, water-quality performance, maintenance requirements, and cost feasibility. While the VR-based evaluation empirically validated prospective resident preferences, particularly the stronger acceptance of the Mixed VF scenario, environmental outcomes such as façade shading, microclimatic improvement, cooling-load reduction, energy reduction, and life-cycle benefits remain potential benefits that should be tested through future simulation, field monitoring, and post-occupancy evaluation.

Future research should follow a multi-dimensional agenda. First, environmental studies should quantify cooling performance, façade-shading effects, energy reduction, evapotranspiration, microclimatic comfort, and seasonal usability under UAE hot-arid conditions. Second, technical studies should test structural loading, waterproofing, drainage, MEP integration, non-potable water separation, nutrient conditioning, irrigation reliability, and system performance across seasons. Third, economic studies should compare capital costs, operation and maintenance costs, affordability impacts, and possible subsidy models for public housing. Fourth, social research should expand the participant profile beyond the current 20–23 prospective-user cohort to include broader age groups, married couples, families with children, elderly residents, current public-housing applicants, and residents from different emirates. Fifth, policy research should examine planning regulations, maintenance governance, usage rights for shared spaces, and incentive mechanisms that can support equitable implementation in UAE affordable/public housing. Overall, the study suggests that vertical farming can add value to Emirati vertical housing when designed as a culturally responsive outdoor living system rather than as a purely technological add-on. The mixed scenario performed best as it combines private and shared spaces and can be linked to building-scale water reuse strategies. The main implication is that future vertical housing in hot-arid regions should integrate farming, shading, water reuse, and socio-cultural spatial patterns within a unified design framework.
